tagline.text: An 1890 Spanish-era red-brick lighthouse overlooking the Verde Island Passage

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Bagong Silang, Calatagan, Batangas, at the southern tip of the Calatagan Peninsula

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱600–1,500 (per person, Manila round-trip bus, tricycle and donation)

children.text: Cape Santiago Lighthouse is a red-brick tower about 15.5 m tall at the southern tip of the Calatagan Peninsula, first lit on December 15, 1890, in the Spanish colonial era. It is known as the oldest working lighthouse in Batangas, and the National Historical Commission placed a landmark marker here in 2018.

Cape Santiago Lighthouse (Spanish name Faro de Cabo Santiago) stands in Barangay Bagong Silang in the city of Calatagan, Batangas. It sits on Cape Santiago, where the Calatagan Peninsula narrows to a point toward the southern sea, about
130 km

southwest of Manila in a straight line. The water in front of it is the Verde Island Passage between Luzon and Mindoro, a route that ships heading into and out of Manila Bay once followed. The lighthouse is a round tower of red brick and lime cement, about
(51 ft) tall, with the keeper's house attached beside it.

It was built as part of the Spanish colonial government's "General Plan of Maritime Lighting" (Plan General de Alumbrado Marítimo), carried out from 1846 to 1896, which aimed to put 55 lighthouses along the archipelago's coasts. In 1887 the Spanish engineer Magin Pers y Pers surveyed the site and recommended a lighthouse here; he is also said to have been involved in the designs of the Cape Bojeador and Cape Engaño lighthouses. Guillermo Brockman designed the tower, the firm Aldecoa y Compañía built it, and it was lit on December 15, 1890. The roughly
1 hectare
site was donated by Don Santiago Zobel, landowner of Hacienda Bigaa, and many accounts say the cape and the lighthouse take their name from him.

The lighthouse is still presented as the oldest working lighthouse in Batangas. It was automated in 1978, so a resident keeper was no longer needed, and over the following decades neglect let it decay and the original light source went missing. Records say the Japanese government donated a bulb through JICA in 1980, and in 1990 the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) renovated the empty keeper's house for use as a tourist inn. On March 12, 2018, the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) installed a marker on site announcing its status as a National Historical Landmark, and the Coast Guard is reported to have begun restoration work in 2021. However, one source records a Notice to Mariners listing the light as unlit as of December 11, 2024, so it is hard to say whether the light is on today. It is best to go expecting to see a building, not a beam of light.

For travelers this is less a grand sight than a quiet place to meet history. A short dirt track off the main road leads in, and you can climb the iron spiral staircase for a view over the Calatagan coast and the sea. Combined with Calatagan's beach resorts, nearby Burot Beach, or the waters of the Verde Island Passage, it makes an easy day trip from Manila. This guide draws on official, press and travel records that could be checked as of 2026, but access and prices change with local conditions, so check the latest information before you go.
The round brick tower has weathered over the years, and where the white paint has peeled the brick shows through. The tower is about
tall, but because it stands on the cape its light is reported to sit about
above sea level. Being part of the Spanish-era lighthouse plan is its greatest value, and up close you can feel the age of the brickwork and the iron railings.

blocks.title: Iron spiral staircase and views from the top

children.text: Inside the tower is a cast-iron spiral staircase, which a visitor account counts as 65 steps. At the top you can see the Calatagan coastline, the blue sea and nearby beaches, with a cool breeze. Safety and access vary by period, so follow the caretaker's guidance, and if you are told you cannot climb, be content with looking from below.

The keeper's house beside the tower is described as keeping a Spanish-era atmosphere in its hallways, old windows and wooden doors. The Coast Guard renovated it in 1990 for tourist use, but there is no confirmed information on whether you can stay there now. If you want to stay overnight, it is safer to look separately at beach resorts in Calatagan.

A marker installed by the National Historical Commission on March 12, 2018, stands on site. Spanish-era lighthouses in the Philippines are better known in the north, such as Cape Bojeador and Cape Engaño, so knowing that southern Luzon's Batangas has a lighthouse from the same plan makes this trip more meaningful.

The sea this lighthouse once lit is the Verde Island Passage between Luzon and Mindoro. On a clear day you can see ships crossing the strait and the distant horizon, and the sky is lovely at sunrise and sunset. The area is known for rich marine life, so for sea lovers the lighthouse visit pairs well with a day on the water.

Burot Beach, on the northwestern coast of the cape, is the place visitor accounts mention most often. It is a mix of sand and shingle, and some people snorkel in its shallow, grassy water. Development is under way, so it may have turned into a private resort; check on site whether you can get in.

items.title: Manila day trip
items.subtitle: Go by morning bus, see the lighthouse and beach, and return

children.text: Take a bus or van to Calatagan from the EDSA-Taft area in Pasay, Manila. One way takes about
3 hours
. First departure times differ by operator, so check the day before.
Get off at the Calatagan public market and take a tricycle to the lighthouse. It is about
10 km
and takes
20–30 minutes
. Agree with the driver on a round-trip fare and waiting time before you set off.
Greet the caretaker at the entrance, leave a donation, then look around the keeper's house and the tower. Spend about
30 minutes
at the top.
Head to a nearby beach for lunch and sea views. Check on site whether Burot Beach is open.
Take the tricycle back to Calatagan town and catch a bus to Manila. Check the last departure time in advance.
The long bus ride makes a day trip tight. Staying one night in Calatagan lets you see the sunrise and the beach at a relaxed pace.

items.title: Two days, one night
items.subtitle: A beach stay in Calatagan and the lighthouse

children.text: Leave Manila and drop your bags at a Calatagan beach lodging around midday. Having a vehicle makes getting around much easier.
Go to the lighthouse, see the tower and keeper's house, and watch the sky at dusk.
Watch the sunrise from the beach and go snorkeling. Leave for Manila after lunch.
Several visitor accounts say buses and vans to Calatagan leave from the EDSA-Taft area in Pasay (near MRT Taft station). The fare in those accounts is about
and the trip takes about
3–4 hours
. Those figures are a few years old and fares have risen on many routes, so confirm locally.
Get off at the Calatagan public market and take a tricycle. Tell the bus conductor in advance to drop you at the "Calatagan Market."
Operators and stops can change, so check the latest information before you leave.
The lighthouse is about
10 km
from town. Chartering a tricycle cost
in visitor accounts (about
if charged per person) for a ride of
20–30 minutes
. It is common to have the same tricycle wait for your return.
The turnoff sign from the main road is on the right side, followed by a dirt track of about
. It turns muddy and slippery in the rain, so take care with your footwear and how you travel.
Reach Calatagan via the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) and the roads toward Batangas. Check the exact route and time on a map app, and avoid heavy-traffic hours.
The entrance track is narrow, so a large vehicle may need to park by the roadside and you walk in.
The lighthouse is an outdoor sight with an unpaved access track, so the dry season with less rain is more comfortable. In the dry season the sea is clearer and the view from the top is better.

For sunrise and sunset photos, go early on a clear day. The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat and water. In the rainy and typhoon seasons the access track turns to mud and strong winds can make climbing risky.

There is no confirmed information on whether you can sleep right next to the lighthouse. The only record is that the keeper's house was renovated for travelers in 1990, and you must check locally whether it still operates. Most travelers stay at beach resorts or campsites in Calatagan and visit the lighthouse during the day. Calatagan is a quiet place without dense resort development, which may not suit anyone wanting a lively resort scene.

There are almost no restaurants around the lighthouse, so bring snacks and water, and eat in Calatagan town or at a beach resort. As in much of Batangas, seafood and grilled meat are common. Prices vary by restaurant, so ask before you order.

One visitor account says the grounds are gated and you can only enter if the caretaker is there. The contact number in that account is old and may have changed, so before you go it is better to ask the Calatagan tourism office whether a visit is possible.
Entry is free, but leaving a donation toward upkeep is good manners. Bring small bills in cash.
Charter the tricycle for a round trip and negotiate the waiting time first. The road is remote, so finding a ride back may be hard.
Before climbing the tower, check the condition of the stairs and railings, and keep hold of children. Avoid slippery shoes.
Bring a hat, sunscreen, water and insect repellent. There are no shops nearby.
Check the last bus time in advance. The last bus from Calatagan to Manila varies by season.
To see both the beach and the lighthouse in one day, start early. If time is short, cut the beach and focus on the lighthouse.
Information conflicts on whether the light is on now and whether a caretaker is there to let you in. Confirm locally that a visit is possible before making the long trip.
One source records the lighthouse as unlit in a December 2024 Notice to Mariners, and the Coast Guard has been carrying out restoration since 2021. Access and lighting can change at any time.
The access track is narrow and unpaved and turns to mud after rain. Motorbikes and tricycles slip easily.
The iron stairs and railings of the tower are old structures. Do not push to climb, and follow the caretaker's guidance.
Records say some places, such as Burot Beach, may be turning into private land, so beach access may be blocked. Check before you go.
The fares and contact numbers in visitor accounts are several years old. They may differ with local conditions, so check the latest notices.
